tldr: This paper presents a palm-sized, completely silent hovercraft that leverages ground proximity effects by attaching a skirt to solid-state ion propulsion (electroaerodynamic propulsion). With a self-mass of about 1.6 g, it achieves a thrust efficiency of 16 mN/W and a payload capacity of nearly 1.5 g, demonstrating stable hovering and disturbance rejection without any active control.
hero_caption: Appearance of the palm-sized ion-propelled micro hovercraft. Composed of a central multistage ion propulsion core and a surrounding thin-film skirt, it achieves sustained tethered hovering and passive attitude stabilization despite having zero moving parts like propellers.
overview:
Micro air vehicles such as drones are expected to work alongside humans in indoor environments, but the hazards and loud noise of high-speed propellers remain major barriers. Electroaerodynamic (EAD) propulsion, which accelerates ions in an electric field to generate airflow, has drawn significant interest as a solution. It operates with zero moving parts and is completely silent. However, its extremely low thrust efficiency has made power-autonomous flight difficult to realize.

The authors focused on the "ground effect" that occurs when an EAD thruster operates in close proximity to the ground. They hypothesized that by attaching a skirt under the propulsion unit to contain the exhaust airflow, they could raise the static pressure beneath the vehicle like a conventional hovercraft and produce substantial lift.

To test this, they built an experimental apparatus capable of systematically varying skirt angle, skirt depth, and center plate placement, thoroughly investigating the resulting changes in thrust and efficiency. The results revealed that pairing an outward-flaring (divergent) skirt with a properly positioned base plate boosted thrust by more than 800% compared to a bare thruster.

Using these findings, the team built a physical vehicle with a self-mass of about 1.6 g that achieves a thrust efficiency of 16 mN/W—an order of magnitude higher than similarly sized EAD robots. Furthermore, the vehicle autonomously recovers its attitude and altitude without any control loops even when poked with a stick, demonstrating remarkable robustness over extended hovering and more than 50 takeoff and landing cycles.
contributions: Proposed and demonstrated the world's first ion-propelled micro hovercraft that actively leverages ground-proximity pressure recovery
Elucidated the effects of skirt geometry (angle, depth, exhaust radius ratio) and base plate placement on thrust and efficiency through systematic experiments
Achieved a thrust efficiency of 16 mN/W and an additional payload capacity of about 1.5 g on a 1.6 g vehicle, outperforming similarly sized EAD robots by an order of magnitude
Demonstrated altitude maintenance and passive recovery from significant disturbances relying solely on the inherent stiffness of the ground effect, without feedback control

sections.heading: Toward a New Floating Robot with No Propellers and No Noise
sections.summary: For small drones, propeller hazards and noise are major obstacles to indoor use. This study overcomes these issues by combining silent, solid-state ion propulsion with a skirt to maximize ground proximity effects, realizing a micro hovercraft.
sections.details:
For small drones sharing spaces with humans, collision risks from rapidly spinning propellers and harsh flight noise are critical drawbacks. To enable humans and robots to coexist comfortably in workplaces and warehouses, quiet and safe alternative propulsion technologies are essential.

Electroaerodynamic (EAD) propulsion is a promising candidate. It ionizes air in strong electric fields, creating wind as accelerated ions collide with neutral air molecules. Because it has no moving parts, it is completely silent and structurally simple. However, conventional free-flying EAD vehicles have suffered from very low thrust efficiency, leaving little prospect for carrying an onboard power supply for autonomous flight.

The breakthrough here lies in leveraging the "ground effect." Fluid-dynamic interactions near walls or the ground are known to enhance thrust, and recent studies have shown that EAD thrusters benefit from ground proximity far more than rotorcraft or flapping-wing vehicles. This study integrates this phenomenon into robot vehicle design for the first time, developing a palm-sized micro hovercraft equipped with a passive skirt.

captions.F2: (a) Architecture of one of the three ion acceleration stages. Ions generated by corona discharge at the emitter tips collide with neutral air, creating a downward flow through the collector grid. (b) Airflow patterns inside the hovercraft. Air impinging on the ground spreads as a wall jet, increasing static pressure within the skirt and generating fountain lift as it recirculates and collides toward the center.

sections.heading: Limitations of Ion Propulsion and the Potential of Ground-Effect Pressure Recovery
sections.summary: Prior EAD robots relied on free-stream thrust and suffered from efficiency limits imposed by space-charge effects. No previous study had applied hovercraft-style skirt confinement to EAD systems, making this work a pioneering effort.
sections.details:
### II-A Electroaerodynamic Propulsion
EAD propulsion produces thrust through momentum transfer between ions and neutral air molecules. While demonstrated in centimeter-scale flyers up to fixed-wing aircraft, previous small-scale EAD robots were all designed for unobstructed flight in free air. Consequently, they were constrained by the physical trade-off of space-charge-limited drift—where increasing thrust reduces efficiency—making extended flight times difficult to achieve.

### II-B Proximity-Mediated Lift Enhancement
Operating near the ground reduces induced downwash velocity and increases lift, creating the "ground effect." Furthermore, confining the downward airflow laterally with a skirt or duct arrests the expanding wall jet along the ground, causing static pressure under the vehicle to surge. While large-scale hovercraft rely on this "pressure-supported cushion," no prior study had combined it with micro-scale EAD propulsion.

### II-C Proximity Effects in Electroaerodynamic Systems
Recent work reported that bringing an isolated EAD thruster near the ground yields thrust amplification surpassing that of rotary-wing vehicles. However, that was limited to fundamental measurements on fixed test rigs; it had never been integrated into a free-flying vehicle structure. This study turns that physical phenomenon into a practical levitating robot.

sections.heading: Multistage Electrode Core and a Millimeter-Precision Test Rig
sections.summary: A 3-stage series ring-shaped ion propulsion core was fabricated with high precision using brass-foil micromachining and 3D printing. An automated test rig modified from a 3D printer evaluated ground effect characteristics by varying skirt angle, depth, and center plate placement.
sections.details:
### III-A Thrusters and Airframe
The propulsion core stacks three ion acceleration stages in series. Each stage consists of an emitter (discharge electrode) and a collector (recovery electrode) separated by a 2 mm gap. Micromachined from 25 μm-thick brass foil using a UV laser, the emitter tips are bent vertically with a stamping die to form sharp needles that sustain stable corona discharge.

The electrodes form a concentric two-ring pattern (40 mm outer diameter) with emitter needles spaced roughly 3 mm apart. To minimize electrostatic interference, adjacent stages are stacked with a 3 mm spacing. To keep weight down, the frame is thin-wall monolithic SLA 3D printed. At the center of the base, an ultra-thin polyetherimide (PEI) center plate of 20 mm diameter is placed within a modular structure that allows flexible adjustments of vertical position $h$, skirt angle $\theta$, and skirt depth $d$.

### III-B Experimental Setup
To measure thrust and electrical characteristics while precisely controlling ground clearance $z$, the authors built an automated test rig by modifying a commercial 3D printer (Ender-3 Pro). A glass ground plate replaced the nozzle, moved with micrometer precision via G-code.

The thruster was mounted face-up (blowing downward toward the ground plate) on a load cell, positioned with ample clearance to avoid ceiling flow reflections. Applying high voltages up to 2.5 kV, the system synchronously logged voltage, ion current, and thrust at 100 ms intervals, comprehensively mapping performance ratios between in-ground-effect (IGE) and out-of-ground-effect (OGE) states.

(b) Laser-micromachined concentric brass patterns for emitter and collector. (c) Exploded assembly view of the 3D-printed airframe, electrodes, and skirt.

sections.heading: Skirt Optimization and an Astonishing Stable Hovering Demo
sections.summary: Flaring the skirt outward and placing the center plate flush with the thruster base greatly enhanced static pressure, thrust, and efficiency. The optimized vehicle hovered stably without active control and remained completely silent, shrugging off mechanical disturbances from a stick.
sections.details:
### IV-A Baseline Ground-Proximity Performance
Testing the bare propulsion core without a skirt near the ground revealed that even at a 1 mm gap, thrust increased by only ~8% and efficiency by ~4%. This alone is far from sufficient to lift the vehicle's self-mass, proving that geometric confinement (a skirt) is essential to capture pressure.

### IV-B Skirt Angle
Comparing skirt angles $\theta$ showed that convergent skirts ($\theta < 0$) choked the flow and degraded thrust, whereas divergent skirts ($\theta > 0$) yielded dramatic gains. At $\theta = 45^{\circ}$, thrust increased by 120% and efficiency rose by 70% in close ground proximity, as the high-pressure region expanded over a larger integrated skirt area.

### IV-C Airframe Center Plate
Evaluating the vertical position $h$ of the central plate revealed that placing it flush with the thruster base ($h = 0$) delivered peak performance. For a $\theta = 65^{\circ}$ skirt, this boosted thrust by over 50% and efficiency by 40% compared to having no plate, as it eliminated dead volume and prevented static pressure leakage. While an intermediate suck-down effect is observed at moderate distances, this actually acts as a natural spring that stabilizes vertical attitude in ultra-low hovercraft flight.

### IV-D Skirt Ratio
Increasing skirt depth $d$ and exhaust radius $R$ monotonically improved thrust and efficiency. In the largest configuration with $\theta = 75^{\circ}$ and a depth of 13.5 mm, thrust surged by ~840% over the bare-thruster baseline. A net excess thrust (payload capacity) of about 1.5 g above vehicle self-mass was confirmed.

### IV-E & IV-F Lift-Off and Hover Demonstration & Characterization
A physical prototype of about 1.6 g was built using this optimal geometry and tested at roughly 2500 V. The vehicle maintained an exceptionally stable hover at a height of 1–2 mm. Even when repeatedly poked and tilted with a stick, it instantly restored its hover height and level attitude without any control loops, stabilized by the passive restorative cushion forces that stiffen near the ground and soften away from it.

The vehicle logged over 10 minutes of continuous flight and 54 takeoff/landing cycles without electrode degradation or arcing, reaching a thrust efficiency of 16 mN/W (over 10 times higher than prior flyers). The authors also proposed an empirical model that captures the steep pressure rise and suck-down behavior unexplained by standard ground-effect formulations (Cheeseman-Bennett).

### IV-G & IV-H Acoustic Signature & Vehicle Dynamics
Compared to a commercial drone (Crazyflie 2.1) and a wheeled robot (HeRo 2.0), the vehicle was so silent that its audio spectrum was entirely buried beneath ambient room HVAC noise. High-speed camera analysis showed smooth, well-damped vertical dynamics with a liftoff velocity of 9.6 mm/s and a touchdown velocity of -7.3 mm/s.

captions.F6: Ground effect differences across skirt angles $\theta$. Convergent skirts ($\theta = -25^{\circ}, -45^{\circ}$) degrade performance, while divergent skirts ($\theta = 25^{\circ}, 45^{\circ}$) dramatically enhance the thrust ratio $F/F_0$ and efficiency ratio $\eta/\eta_0$ near the ground ($z/r < 0.2$).
captions.F7: Impact of center plate height $h$ and skirt angle on thrust and efficiency. The flush configuration ($h = 0$) achieves the highest performance, contributing significantly to pressure retention near the ground. The lower panel highlights the suck-down regime where the thrust ratio drops below 1 at intermediate distances.
captions.F8: Thrust ratio, efficiency, net thrust $F_{net}$, and areal thrust density versus skirt exhaust radius ratio $R/r$. Expanding the exhaust radius monotonically increases thrust and efficiency, yielding over 10 mN of excess net thrust beyond vehicle weight at the maximum $\theta = 75^{\circ}$ configuration.

sections.heading: Challenges Toward Full Autonomy and Real-World Deployment
sections.summary: Because the vehicle currently depends on an external tethered power source, integrating ultra-lightweight high-voltage DC-DC converters is the primary hurdle for autonomy. Further optimization of thruster geometries and understanding uneven surface interactions remain future work.
sections.details:
While this study achieves a major milestone, several critical challenges remain.

- **Power autonomy**: Flight is currently tethered to an external high-voltage source via fine wires. Untethered autonomous mobility requires integrating gram-scale, ultra-lightweight high-voltage DC-DC converters and small batteries onto the airframe.
- **Thruster core exploration**: Electrode gaps and ring diameters were kept fixed based on prior literature; co-optimizing electrode parameters specifically for ground-effect hovercraft could yield further efficiency gains.
- **Surface condition sensitivity**: Experiments were conducted over a smooth glass sheet. In real-world environments, floor roughness, gaps, and obstacles could break the air cushion seal under the skirt, requiring tests of terrain robustness.
- **Planar translation and steering**: Only vertical hovering and passive stability were demonstrated here. Moving forward and turning will require active steering mechanisms, such as circumferentially segmenting the electrodes for thrust vectoring.

sections.heading: Conclusion: Opening a New Door for Silent Flying Microrobots
sections.summary: By actively exploiting ground-effect pressure recovery, the team realized a completely silent ion-propelled micro hovercraft achieving a thrust efficiency of 16 mN/W. This work lays the design foundation for a new class of low-altitude, silent microrobots.
sections.details:
This study marks the first successful design and flight demonstration of an ion-propelled micro hovercraft capable of sustained levitation with practically zero audible noise and no moving parts.

With an optimized geometry featuring a skirt angle of $\theta = 75^{\circ}$ and a depth of $d = 13.5$ mm, the vehicle boosted thrust by over 800% relative to a bare thruster, providing ~1.5 g of additional payload capacity over its 1.6 g self-mass. Moreover, aerodynamic damping inherent to ground proximity enabled passive hover stabilization and disturbance rejection without any active control circuitry.

These findings open a completely new pathway for small-scale EAD propulsion, which has long struggled with insufficient efficiency for practical flight. It represents a definitive step toward silent, intrinsically safe human-collaborative micro air vehicles for indoor environments.

takeaways: Propulsion methods limited by low thrust density can achieve practical lift when paired with ground effect and skirt-based pressure recovery
Combining an outward-flaring (divergent) skirt with a flush base plate plays a decisive role in building up underbody static pressure
Nonlinear restorative forces (cushion effects) near the ground enable passive disturbance rejection without microcontrollers or active feedback
Unlike motors and propellers, EAD propulsion possesses the unique advantage of complete silence, blending entirely into ambient HVAC noise
limitations: Requires a tethered connection to an external high-voltage source (~2500 V); fully untethered flight has not yet been achieved
Hover height is extremely low (1–2 mm), making the air cushion prone to leakage over uneven surfaces or steps
Active thrust-vectoring or steering mechanisms for planar translation and yaw control have not yet been implemented
